assumptions: The venture remains a verification and origination intermediary and does not deploy the founder's capital or retain principal credit risk.
Any beneficiary data, installer records, and family-company workflow access are used only with explicit lawful consent and without employer resources.
At least one payment stream can be financed under a structure acceptable to Polish counsel and a licensed funding provider.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A counsel-reviewed transaction structure, one funder term sheet, and a cohort of real installer files showing receivable size, cash-gap duration, approval rate, fraud and defect rate, all-in funding cost, installer willingness to pay, processing labor, and repeat volume.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The program-specific wedge is coherent: partial prefinancing and documentation-gated final payment can create a financeable contractor cash-flow gap. The underlying insight is useful but not intrinsically novel, because working-capital finance and receivables broking already address similar gaps.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Materials, payroll, and distributor deadlines can make delayed reimbursement materially painful for a small installer, and a funded transaction is a concrete outcome. However, the 35% advance mitigates some need, and there is no transaction-level evidence yet on delay duration, avoided loss, desired advance, or willingness to pay the proposed fee.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: An origination or verification fee can be capital-light and attractive when deal sizes are large, while avoiding founder balance-sheet lending. Margin and owner earnings remain highly uncertain because each case may require manual document and fraud review, partner revenue sharing, compliance overhead, rejection handling, and delayed success-fee collection.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish Clean Air installers form a legible initial segment with repeat project flow, and a specific receivable is a suitably narrow beachhead transaction. The packet does not establish the number, value, concentration, or financeability of eligible receivables, and dependence on one subsidy program limits confidence in the segment's durable economic size.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Specialized normalization across multiple funders could earn a niche position if incumbents handle these files poorly. Banks, factors, distributors, program operators, and vertical brokers already own relevant relationships and can internalize intake, while the proposed one-transaction exclusivity does not create segment domination by itself.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven verification and routing engine could extend to other installer categories, subsidy-backed work, and related SME receivables. Expansion is plausible but not automatic because each payment stream may have distinct assignment, consent, fraud, and funder-underwriting rules.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Permissioned defect, exception, and repayment outcomes could improve triage over time. No data rights, exclusive channel, funding capacity, or durable contract are secured, individual origination rights expire with each deal, and rule changes or incumbent replication could erode the advantage quickly.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A single verified packet routed transparently to several lawful funders could improve speed and approval cost versus unstructured applications. The magnitude is unmeasured, free operator support weakens documentation as a standalone differentiator, and the offer has little value if the payment stream is not acceptable collateral.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Current rules expose a staged cash-flow window, and the longer completion allowance can increase the period during which working capital matters. At the same time, subsidy-program specialization creates policy volatility, and the evidence does not show that private funders are moving into this asset now.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installation firm can support a consent-based workflow pilot, while accountants, distributors, associations, and finance partners are credible routes to installers. Repeatable acquisition still requires convincing both receivable owners and licensed funders, and each proposed channel can preserve or internalize the customer relationship.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A document-readiness pilot fits the founder's analytical skills, time, and capital if lending remains external. Commercial launch depends on legal characterization, assignability or collateral acceptance, beneficiary consent, fraud controls, data protection, and at least one committed funder, creating substantial non-software execution risk for a part-time founder.

highest_value_structural_change: Secure a licensed funder's conditional term sheet for one narrowly defined receivable class and redesign the offer around that funder's approved eligibility, consent, recourse, pricing, and document rules before selling broad routing.
main_structural_strength: A concrete, document-defined cash-flow event can support a capital-light fee model tied to actual funding rather than a generic software subscription.
primary_score_limiter: The proposed product has not established that the relevant subsidy or contract payment stream is legally financeable on terms that leave enough value for both the installer and the intermediary.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Existing 35% program prefinancing and free operator assistance reduce two parts of the claimed gap, while subsidy eligibility itself does not establish assignability or collateral value.
